newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Cash cocoa trade patchy at best in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Cash cocoa trade patchy at best in Europe.

text.p: Cash cocoa activity in Europe remained patchy at best this week with many players lamenting the slack industry offtake, although a few reported a slight pick-up in business in the last few days.

Sterling's rise against other European currencies this year was still cited as a major deterrent to trade and the chocolate industry's continued reluctance to make fresh purchases indicated that at least the major buyers remained well covered.
"The market is quieter than I've ever seen it," said one senior trader based in continental Europe. "Business is tough, very tough."
Traders said the world coffee market, surging to 20-year highs on supply worries, had also helped take the spotlight away from cocoa and discouraged some participation.

Origin selling was limited to small amounts of business, with the Ivory Coast and Cameroon reported to be in the market, offering new crop cocoa. A recent report from German traders Albrecht & Dill estimated the Ivorians to have sold up to 600,000 tonnes or even more of the 1997/98 (October-September) main crop.

Some traders commented on unconfirmed reports that a large tonnage, allegedly around 120,000 tonnes, of cocoa had recently been deblocked in Abidjan for shipment next year. Others gave the rumours little credence.

One trader said that after an extremely quiet month, dealing had perked up recently. He noted deals in Ivorian and Nigerian cocoa as well as some of the finer grades for positions next year and into 1999, all with chocolate manufacturers.
"This is business we have yet to hedge on the terminal market," he said, declining to specify the tonnages or differentials involved.
Others said differentials had not moved from last week.

Quality problems were still a talking point, with at least one trade house in continental Europe, reportedly losing out on a major shipment, which although bought at a discount to the prevailing physical market, turned out to be unusable.

But the main factor affecting trading levels is the lack of demand on the part of industry -- with offtake for beans and butter said to be at historically low levels. Sterling strength and the seasonal rumours over the size of West African crops, were cited as principal factors.
"Chocolate makers have no appetite for the market at its current levels," one UK trader commented.
"No one is in a hurry to do anything until the silly season is over."
